title: What Banks Do
objective: After this level you can explain how banks take deposits and make loans.
summary: Banks grew out of medieval money changers' benches. A bank takes deposits and makes loans, standing between savers and borrowers, and earns on the spread between the two interest rates.

cards.headline: Why is it called a bank? Blame a wooden bench.
cards.body: In medieval Italy, money changers did business at a banco, a bench or table. Along the way they invented the job every bank still does.

cards.headline: Deposits in, loans out
cards.body: Lombard money changers started out swapping coins for foreign merchants and travelers. Then clients began leaving money with them for safekeeping, and anyone who wanted to borrow could come to the changer, who lent those deposits out. That's still the heart of banking: a bank accepts deposits and makes loans.

cards.headline: The middleman
cards.body: Economists call a bank a financial intermediary. It sits between savers who deposit money and borrowers who take out loans. Without one, a saver with spare cash would have to hunt down someone who wanted to borrow it and trust them to pay it back. Remember barter's lucky match from Level 2? A bank spares savers and borrowers from having to find each other.

cards.fact: A bank earns its living in the gap between two interest rates.
cards.context: It pays interest on deposits and charges a higher rate on its loans. The difference is called the spread, and it covers the bank's costs and its profit. The benches got fancier over the centuries. The business model barely changed.

mascot.line: Keep this: a bank borrows at one rate and lends at a higher one. The spread is its living.

cards.headline: Banks: explained
learned: The word bank comes from the Italian banco, a bench
Banks take deposits and make loans
They stand between savers and borrowers
They earn on the spread between loan and deposit rates

questions.prompt: At its core, what two things does a bank do?

options.label: Prints banknotes and sets shop prices
options.rationale: Banks take deposits and lend; they don't set shop prices.

options.label: Collects taxes and pays pensions
options.rationale: That's government work, not a bank's core job.

options.label: Buys gold and stores it in vaults
options.rationale: Storing gold isn't the heart of banking; lending deposits is.

questions.explanation: A bank accepts deposits from savers and makes loans to borrowers: it is a financial intermediary.

questions.prompt: How does a bank make money from lending?

options.label: It charges borrowers more interest than it pays depositors
It keeps a fee from every coin it exchanges
options.rationale: That was the money changers' old trade, not the lending business.

options.label: It pays depositors more interest than it charges borrowers
options.rationale: That would lose money: the loan rate is the higher one.

options.label: The government pays it for each new account
options.rationale: Its income comes from the spread between the two rates.

questions.explanation: The spread between the higher loan rate and the lower deposit rate covers the bank's costs and profit.

questions.prompt: A medieval Lombard money changer lent out his clients' deposits. What modern role was he playing?

options.label: A tax collector for the local ruler
options.rationale: He was matching savers' money with borrowers, not collecting taxes.

options.label: A shopkeeper selling goods on credit
options.rationale: He dealt in money, not goods.

options.label: A mint stamping new coins
options.rationale: Minting coins is a state job; he was lending deposits.

options.label: A financial intermediary between savers and borrowers

questions.explanation: Taking deposits and lending them out is exactly what makes a bank a financial intermediary.
